contents.title: Stack Operations
contents.definition: A stack stores data in last-in, first-out order, so the most recently inserted item is removed first.
contents.realLifeExample: A stack of plates works the same way because the top plate is the first one taken out.

contents.title: Linked Stack PUSH
contents.definition: Linked stack push inserts a new node at the front of the linked stack and makes it the new top.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like placing one more book on top of a pile and treating that book as the new top item.

contents.title: Linked Stack POP
contents.definition: Linked stack pop removes the node at the top of the stack and shifts the top pointer to the next node.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like removing the top card from a deck and revealing the next card below it.

contents.title: Evaluation of a Postfix Expression
contents.definition: Postfix evaluation scans an expression from left to right and uses a stack to hold operands until an operator can be applied.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like keeping numbers on a scratch pad until an arithmetic sign tells you which two values to combine.

contents.title: Infix to Postfix (POLISH)
contents.definition: The POLISH algorithm converts an infix expression into postfix form by using a stack for operators and parentheses.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like temporarily holding operation signs until the output order is safe and unambiguous.

contents.title: Infix to Prefix
contents.definition: Infix to prefix conversion reverses the expression, swaps parentheses, uses a stack conversion pass, and reverses the result.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like reading the expression from the other side, arranging operators by priority, then flipping the answer back.

contents.title: Linear Queue Insertion and Deletion
contents.definition: A linear queue follows first-in, first-out order and uses front and rear positions to track deletion and insertion.
contents.realLifeExample: People standing in a ticket line behave like a queue because the first person to enter is the first person served.

contents.title: Circular Queue Insertion and Deletion
contents.definition: A circular queue reuses empty spaces by wrapping front and rear back to the beginning when they reach the end.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like seats arranged in a circle where the next available place may come again at the beginning.

contents.title: Linked List as Queue Insertion and Deletion
contents.definition: A linked queue stores queue items in linked nodes so insertions happen at the rear and deletions happen at the front.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like adding a new person at the back of a line while the person at the front leaves when served.

contents.title: Priority Queue (One-dimensional Array)
contents.definition: A priority queue removes the highest-priority item first even if that item was not inserted first.
contents.realLifeExample: Emergency patients are treated before regular patients, so priority decides who goes first.

contents.title: Priority Queue (Two-dimensional Array)
contents.definition: A two-dimensional priority queue keeps separate storage for each priority level and processes higher priorities first.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like having separate service lines for urgent, normal, and low-priority tasks.

contents.title: Deque
contents.definition: A deque allows insertion and deletion from both the front and the rear of the structure.
contents.realLifeExample: It is like a line where people are allowed to enter or leave from either side.
